turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late, the luas from rathmines was jammed solid and I dumped coffee down my coat. Mortified, honestly.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand. The coat'll dry. I'm Dr Brennan, sit in there the both of you.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm her mam, Orla. Sure I only came along so she wouldn't turn at the door. We did two laps of the car park, it's a disgrace.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): It is, these days. So, what brought you in?

[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Em, we were down in Galway for my cousin's hen at the weekend and the girls were all on about coils, and I hadn't a notion. Umm, but that's not it. I want to sort out contraception, I've been putting it off.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Contraception. What have you used before, if anything?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): The pill. Uh, microlyte, the little low dose one. I was on it for about four months. That was last year.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Microlite, yes. And why did you stop?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Headaches. They were rotten, like a tight band, two or three days a week. I came off it and they went, thank god.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ok. With those headaches, any flashing lights, or zigzags in the vision?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): I work in a cafe on Georges Street. Early shifts, I'm wrecked half the time. That's why I was so snappy, I reckon.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Early shifts would wreck anyone. The flashing lights though, did you actually get them?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No lights, no zigzags. Just the thumping pain, and it was gone once I quit the pill.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was in bits on the couch those evenings, I'm not going to lie. But once she stopped that pill she was back to herself.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grand, so they settled. Are you on any tablets now, prescribed or just over the counter?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I don't even bother with paracetamol unless I'm desperate.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm. No, nothing that I know of.

[SEG0019] person_4 (NURSE): I'll grab the blood pressure while ye are talking. My sister got the implant last spring and she texted me a photo of the bruise, looked like she'd played a full hurling match. Arm out, love.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh god. Does it always bruise like that? My friend said hers was nothing.
[SEG0021] person_4 (NURSE): Not always, no. Right. One twenty four over seventy eight. Pulse is seventy two. That's a lovely reading.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Niamh. One twenty four over seventy eight, pulse seventy two. Reassuring for today.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Periods are dead regular, every 28 days, four days, not heavy at all.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's useful to know. I did ask about the cigarettes, though.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, sorry. Yeah, I smoke, only occasionally. Three or four on a night out, and not even every week. I'm not a smoker smoker.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She had two at the hen, I saw her. That's about the height of it.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with your breathing, or with your chest, at the moment?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Chest is grand. I can leg it for the luas, no bother.

[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back so I've got it. You want contraception, Microlite for about four months last year brought rotten headaches with no flashing lights and they went when you stopped, and I'd put those headaches down to the pill. No other tablets, no allergies you know of, periods regular, pressure grand today, and a few cigarettes on a night out.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's me. Sorry, I do wander off.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not a bother. The combined pill has oestrogen in it, and oestrogen can make the blood a little stickier. Even the odd cigarette on top of that pushes the clot risk up, so I wouldn't start you back on Microlite or any combined pill.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Fair enough. So what can I actually use? I don't want the injection, my cousin piled the weight on with that yoke.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): The ones that suit better are the progesterone only pill, the implant in the arm, or a coil. The implant lasts three years, and we can take it out if it doesn't suit.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): The implant sounds handy, I forget pills. Umm. Will it wreck my skin?

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Some people get a bit of acne, or bleeding that's all over the place, and some get neither. I can't tell which you'd be. I'll give you the implant leaflet today so you've got it in front of you.
[SEG0037] person_4 (NURSE): I've it here. The Nexplanon leaflet. Have a proper read before you're back.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She'll read it at the kitchen table, not on the bus. I'll see to that.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I not just decide today? I kind of want it done and dusted.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd sooner you decide at the next visit, once you've read it. We'll book you back in two weeks and you can tell me then. If you do have the implant and the bleeding hasn't settled after three months, we might do an ultrasound. Any chest pain or breathlessness in the meantime, don't sit on it, come back or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Grand. I'll read it, I promise. Two weeks so. Thanks.

spec.situation: Young woman asks about contraception, previous pill caused headaches, smokes occasionally; blood pressure read; options discussed; implant leaflet given, decision next visit.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
